Kinematics Consider forces involved: Direction Speed Energy transfer Deceleration Rotation Compression Penetration Crush forces Potential injuries should be predicted from the mechanism and then confirmed or excluded through assessment. 6. Primary Trauma Assessment The primary assessment should rapidly identify conditions that threaten life. Airway Assess: Patency Ability to protect airway Obstruction Facial trauma Blood/vomitus Dental injury Burns Swelling Neck injury Breathing Assess: Respiratory effort Rate Chest movement Lung sounds Oxygenation Ventilation Chest wall injury Open chest wounds Signs of tension physiology Circulation Assess: Major external hemorrhage Pulse Skin Perfusion Mental status Signs of shock Pelvic injury Internal hemorrhage Disability Assess: Mental status GCS when appropriate Pupils Motor function Sensory findings Focal neurologic deficits Blood glucose when indicated Exposure Expose enough to identify life-threatening injuries while preventing: Hypothermia Loss of dignity Unnecessary exposure 7. Major Hemorrhage Major hemorrhage is a time-critical trauma problem. Look for: Spurting bleeding Persistent bleeding Large-volume blood loss Blood-soaked clothing Partial or complete amputation Junctional bleeding Deep wounds Pelvic injury Signs of shock Current NAEMSP guidance includes a dedicated position statement on prehospital hemorrhage control and treatment. 8. Hemorrhage Control Training should cover: Direct pressure Pressure dressings Tourniquets Wound packing Hemostatic dressings when authorized Junctional hemorrhage control Reassessment The AI should always distinguish between: What is clinically appropriate and What the local EMS protocol authorizes. 9. Tourniquet Training Training should cover: Indications Proper placement Tightening Confirmation of hemorrhage control Documentation Reassessment Time documentation Complications The AI should not invent a local agency's preferred tourniquet brand or protocol. 10. Shock Trauma can cause multiple types of shock. Important categories include: Hemorrhagic shock Blood loss → reduced circulating volume → reduced perfusion. Obstructive shock Examples include: Tension pneumothorax Cardiac tamponade Neurogenic shock May occur with significant spinal cord injury and has a distinct physiology from hemorrhagic shock. Facial Trauma Assess for: Airway compromise Facial fractures Bleeding Dental injury Loose teeth Foreign bodies Eye injury Nasal injury Midface instability Mandibular injury Facial trauma can rapidly become an airway problem. 15. Cervical Spine / Spinal Trauma Assess: Mechanism Neck pain Midline tenderness Neurologic symptoms Weakness Numbness Paresthesias Deformity Altered mental status Distracting injuries Current consensus uses the term spinal motion restriction (SMR) rather than implying that EMS can completely immobilize the spine. NAEMSP's published guidance identifies factors including altered consciousness, midline neck/back pain or tenderness, focal neurologic findings, spinal deformity, and distracting injuries as indications in blunt trauma. Important: Your AI should use the patient's actual local trauma/SMR protocol when deciding whether SMR is indicated. 16. Pelvic Trauma Consider significant pelvic injury with mechanisms such as: High-energy collision Crush injury Significant fall Pedestrian impact Look for: Pelvic pain Instability when clinically appropriate Lower abdominal pain Perineal bruising Leg-length abnormalities Shock Associated injuries Avoid unnecessary repeated manipulation of a potentially unstable pelvis. Inhalation Injury Consider with: Enclosed-space fire Facial burns Soot Hoarseness Stridor Carbonaceous sputum Respiratory distress Altered mental status Airway edema can progress over time. 29. Chemical Burns Training should address: Scene safety Decontamination Removal of contaminated clothing Eye exposure Respiratory exposure Chemical identification when safely available Poison-control resources when appropriate Specific decontamination procedures should follow the substance-specific guidance and local protocol. 30. Pediatric Trauma Pediatric trauma requires consideration of: Age Weight Anatomy Development Mechanism Vital signs appropriate for age Airway size Medication dosing Equipment size Abuse/neglect The AI should never automatically apply adult trauma thresholds to children. 32. Geriatric Trauma Older adults may have serious injury with apparently minor mechanisms. Trauma Triage Trauma triage should consider: Physiologic criteria Anatomic injuries Mechanism Special considerations Age Resources Trauma-center capability Destination criteria must come from the applicable regional trauma system. Repeat: Airway Breathing Circulation Hemorrhage Mental status Vital signs Neurovascular status Pain Treatment response A stable trauma patient can become unstable. 38. Secondary Trauma Survey A systematic head-to-toe assessment may include: Head Scalp Skull Face Eyes Ears Nose Mouth Neck Cervical tenderness Deformity Vascular findings Chest Inspection Palpation Auscultation Abdomen Inspection Palpation Distention Tenderness Pelvis Injury findings Bleeding Extremities Deformity Pulses Motor Sensory Posterior Assess when appropriate and when it can be done safely. 39. Recommended Source Material For your actual Trauma folder, I would prioritize current, authoritative documents rather than filling it with random EMS websites. Useful categories include: Local EMS trauma protocols Regional trauma-system guidelines State EMS protocols Medical-director policies Current trauma-system triage criteria NAEMSP trauma position statements ACS Committee on Trauma resources Relevant peer-reviewed trauma literature NAEMSP's current trauma collection is particularly useful because it includes recent resources on traumatic cardiac arrest, spinal cord injuries, pelvic fractures, femoral shaft fractures, geriatric trauma, hemorrhage control, and TXA. 51. Pediatric Assessment and Initial Management 1. Purpose This document provides a structured framework for the prehospital assessment and initial management of pediatric patients. It is intended to support paramedics and a documentation-grounded paramedic AI in recognizing pediatric illness, identifying deterioration, selecting appropriate assessment priorities, and locating the appropriate pediatric protocol. Current local EMS protocols, medical-director orders, pediatric medication protocols, scope of practice, manufacturer instructions, and applicable law take precedence over this general reference. The 2025 American Heart Association (AHA) and American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) pediatric guidelines address pediatric patients in prearrest, intra-arrest, and post-arrest states and include pediatric BLS and advanced life support. 2. Pediatric Age Definitions The AI should identify the patient's developmental category before providing pediatric-specific recommendations. For 2025 AHA pediatric BLS guidance: Infant Approximately younger than 1 year of age, excluding newborn infants. Child Approximately 1 year of age until puberty. Puberty and older Patients showing signs of puberty should generally follow adult BLS guidance. The pediatric BLS guidelines specifically exclude newborn infants, whose resuscitation follows neonatal guidance because of their unique transition from fetal to neonatal physiology. Local EMS definitions may differ and should take precedence. 3. Pediatric Assessment Principles Pediatric assessment should rapidly determine: Is the child critically ill? Is the airway patent? Is breathing adequate? Is oxygenation adequate? Is ventilation adequate? Is circulation adequate? Is the child in shock? Is the child at risk for respiratory failure? Is the child experiencing cardiac arrest? What is the most likely underlying cause? Pediatric patients may compensate for significant illness before suddenly deteriorating. Early recognition of respiratory failure and shock is therefore important. 4. Pediatric Appearance Assess the child's overall appearance. Consider: Level of consciousness Interaction with caregivers Muscle tone Ability to respond appropriately Eye contact Speech or cry Consolability Work of breathing Skin color Position A markedly abnormal appearance may indicate serious illness even before severe vital-sign abnormalities develop. 5. Pediatric Respiratory Assessment Assess: Respiratory rate Respiratory effort Chest movement Breath sounds Air entry Oxygen saturation Skin color Mental status Ability to speak or cry Presence of abnormal airway sounds Potential signs of respiratory distress

Speech or cry Consolability Work of breathing Skin color Position A markedly abnormal appearance may indicate serious illness even before severe vital-sign abnormalities develop. 5. Pediatric Respiratory Assessment Assess: Respiratory rate Respiratory effort Chest movement Breath sounds Air entry Oxygen saturation Skin color Mental status Ability to speak or cry Presence of abnormal airway sounds Potential signs of respiratory distress include: Tachypnea Nasal flaring Retractions Grunting Accessory-muscle use Head bobbing in infants Abnormal positioning Wheezing Stridor Crackles Decreased air movement Cyanosis Potential signs of respiratory failure include: Decreasing mental status Severe fatigue Poor respiratory effort Apnea Bradycardia Cyanosis Inadequate chest movement Inability to maintain oxygenation or ventilation Respiratory conditions are a major cause of pediatric cardiac arrest, making early support of oxygenation and ventilation particularly important. 6. Pediatric Airway Assess for: Airway obstruction Secretions Vomitus Blood Foreign body Tongue obstruction Facial trauma Airway swelling Anaphylaxis Burns or inhalation injury Altered mental status Basic airway interventions may include: Positioning Airway-opening maneuvers Suction Airway adjuncts Oxygen Assisted ventilation Advanced airway interventions should follow the applicable pediatric airway protocol and provider scope. 7. Pediatric Ventilation If a pediatric patient has inadequate or absent breathing, ventilation support should be initiated promptly. The 2025 AHA pediatric BLS guidelines emphasize rapid support of ventilation and oxygenation in seriously ill children. Potential interventions include: Appropriate airway positioning Supplemental oxygen when indicated Bag-valve-mask ventilation Advanced airway management when indicated Continuous reassessment Avoid both inadequate and excessive ventilation. 8. Pediatric Oxygenation Assess oxygenation using: Clinical appearance Pulse oximetry Work of breathing Skin color Mental status Oxygen therapy should follow the applicable pediatric respiratory protocol. Do not use pulse oximetry as the sole indicator of respiratory status. A child can have significant respiratory distress before oxygen saturation becomes severely abnormal. 9. Pediatric Circulation Assess: Heart rate Pulse quality Blood pressure when appropriate Capillary refill when useful Skin temperature Skin color Mental status Urine output when history is available Signs of shock Pediatric patients can maintain blood pressure despite significant circulatory compromise. Therefore, normal blood pressure does not automatically exclude shock. 10. Pediatric Shock Consider shock when there is evidence of

9. Pediatric Circulation Assess: Heart rate Pulse quality Blood pressure when appropriate Capillary refill when useful Skin temperature Skin color Mental status Urine output when history is available Signs of shock Pediatric patients can maintain blood pressure despite significant circulatory compromise. Therefore, normal blood pressure does not automatically exclude shock. 10. Pediatric Shock Consider shock when there is evidence of inadequate tissue perfusion. Potential findings include: Tachycardia Weak peripheral pulses Delayed capillary refill Cool extremities Pale or mottled skin Altered mental status Decreased urine output Hypotension Increasing respiratory distress Abnormal skin temperature Potential causes include: Hypovolemic shock Examples: Hemorrhage Dehydration Vomiting Diarrhea Burns Distributive shock Examples: Sepsis Anaphylaxis Cardiogenic shock Examples: Myocarditis Cardiomyopathy Congenital heart disease Dysrhythmia Obstructive shock Examples: Tension pneumothorax Cardiac tamponade Pulmonary embolism Treatment should follow the appropriate pediatric shock protocol and underlying cause. The 2025 PALS guidelines specifically address pediatric shock and different shock etiologies. 11. Pediatric Vital Signs Vital signs should be interpreted according to: Age Clinical condition Activity Fever Medications Baseline health Local pediatric reference ranges The AI should not automatically apply adult normal ranges to pediatric patients. A heart rate that is normal for an infant may be abnormal for an adolescent. 12. Pediatric Heart Rate Evaluate: Rate Rhythm Regularity Pulse quality Relationship to clinical condition Perfusion Tachycardia may be: Physiologic Related to fever Related to pain Related to dehydration Related to hypoxia Related to shock Caused by a primary arrhythmia Bradycardia in a seriously ill child may indicate significant hypoxia or respiratory failure. 13. Pediatric Cardiac Arrest Pediatric cardiac arrest is frequently associated with respiratory failure or shock rather than an isolated primary cardiac event. When cardiac arrest is recognized: Begin high-quality CPR. Provide effective ventilation. Apply the monitor/defibrillator. Identify the rhythm. Defibrillate shockable rhythms when indicated. Establish vascular access. Administer appropriate medications according to current pediatric protocol. Identify and treat reversible causes. Reassess continuously. The 2025 pediatric BLS guidance emphasizes conventional CPR with both compressions and ventilations for infants and children in cardiac arrest. 14. Pediatric CPR For pediatric cardiac arrest, use current pediatric resuscitation guidance. The 2025 AHA/AAP pediatric BLS

Defibrillate shockable rhythms when indicated. Establish vascular access. Administer appropriate medications according to current pediatric protocol. Identify and treat reversible causes. Reassess continuously. The 2025 pediatric BLS guidance emphasizes conventional CPR with both compressions and ventilations for infants and children in cardiac arrest. 14. Pediatric CPR For pediatric cardiac arrest, use current pediatric resuscitation guidance. The 2025 AHA/AAP pediatric BLS guidelines recommend: Compression rate of approximately 100–120/min Compression depth of approximately one-third of the anterior-posterior chest diameter Approximately 4 cm for infants Approximately 5 cm for children Minimizing interruptions Complete chest recoil For infants, the 2025 guidelines no longer recommend the 2-finger compression technique because of concerns about achieving adequate depth; 1-hand or 2-thumb–encircling-hands techniques are recommended. 15. Pediatric AED/Defibrillation Use an AED or manual defibrillator as soon as available during pediatric cardiac arrest. When available, a pediatric attenuator may be used according to current guidance and equipment instructions. The 2025 AHA/AAP pediatric BLS guidelines recommend immediate AED application/use for pediatric cardiac arrest when available, including use of a pediatric attenuator when available. Defibrillation energy should come from the current pediatric resuscitation protocol and device-specific guidance. 16. Pediatric Advanced Life Support PALS-level management may include: Advanced airway management Vascular access Weight-based medication administration Defibrillation Cardioversion Pacing when indicated Treatment of bradycardia Treatment of tachyarrhythmias Shock management Post-cardiac-arrest care The 2025 PALS guidelines specifically address airway management, ventilation, medication administration, defibrillation, shock, bradycardia, tachycardia, congenital heart disease, and post-arrest care. 17. Pediatric Bradycardia Evaluate: Heart rate Oxygenation Ventilation Mental status Perfusion Blood pressure ECG rhythm In a critically ill child, bradycardia should prompt immediate assessment of oxygenation and ventilation. Potential causes include: Hypoxia Respiratory failure Increased vagal tone Medication effects Hypothermia Metabolic abnormalities Cardiac disease Treatment should follow the current pediatric bradycardia algorithm. 18. Pediatric Tachycardia Determine whether tachycardia is likely: Sinus tachycardia Supraventricular tachycardia Another atrial rhythm Ventricular tachycardia Secondary to another illness Assess: Heart rate Rhythm regularity QRS width P waves Clinical symptoms Perfusion Blood pressure Underlying illness A fast heart rate in a sick child should not automatically be labeled SVT. Pain, fever, hypoxia, dehydration, and shock can

bradycardia algorithm. 18. Pediatric Tachycardia Determine whether tachycardia is likely: Sinus tachycardia Supraventricular tachycardia Another atrial rhythm Ventricular tachycardia Secondary to another illness Assess: Heart rate Rhythm regularity QRS width P waves Clinical symptoms Perfusion Blood pressure Underlying illness A fast heart rate in a sick child should not automatically be labeled SVT. Pain, fever, hypoxia, dehydration, and shock can all produce sinus tachycardia. 19. Pediatric Respiratory Emergencies The pediatric folder should contain dedicated documents for: Asthma Bronchiolitis Croup Upper-airway obstruction Foreign-body airway obstruction Pneumonia Respiratory failure Anaphylaxis Inhalation injury Drowning Pneumothorax Severe respiratory distress 20. Foreign-Body Airway Obstruction Assess whether the obstruction is: Mild/partial Severe/complete The 2025 pediatric BLS guidelines provide different interventions for infants and children with severe foreign-body airway obstruction. For infants with severe obstruction, the current guideline uses repeated cycles of 5 back blows followed by 5 chest thrusts. For children with severe obstruction, the guideline uses repeated cycles of 5 back blows followed by 5 abdominal thrusts. Blind finger sweeps should not be performed. If the patient becomes unresponsive, initiate CPR according to the current pediatric algorithm and remove a visible foreign body when opening the airway. 21. Pediatric Asthma Assess: Respiratory rate Work of breathing Air movement Wheezing Mental status Oxygenation Ability to speak Fatigue Severe asthma may progress to respiratory failure. Concerning findings include: Minimal air movement Altered mental status Exhaustion Cyanosis Bradycardia Silent chest Treatment should follow the local pediatric respiratory protocol. 22. Croup and Upper-Airway Obstruction Assess for: Barking cough Stridor Hoarseness Retractions Drooling Difficulty swallowing Abnormal positioning Increasing respiratory distress Avoid unnecessarily agitating a child with significant upper-airway obstruction. Consider alternative diagnoses when presentation is atypical. 23. Anaphylaxis Pediatric anaphylaxis may involve: Airway swelling Stridor Wheezing Respiratory distress Hypotension Poor perfusion Hives Angioedema Gastrointestinal symptoms Epinephrine is the primary medication treatment when indicated. Additional treatments should follow the local pediatric anaphylaxis protocol. The 2025 AHA special-circumstances guidelines include pediatric considerations for anaphylaxis. 24. Pediatric Seizures Assess: Seizure duration Generalized vs focal activity Current mental status Respiratory status Blood glucose Temperature Trauma Medication history Known seizure disorder Possible toxicologic cause Potential

perfusion Hives Angioedema Gastrointestinal symptoms Epinephrine is the primary medication treatment when indicated. Additional treatments should follow the local pediatric anaphylaxis protocol. The 2025 AHA special-circumstances guidelines include pediatric considerations for anaphylaxis. 24. Pediatric Seizures Assess: Seizure duration Generalized vs focal activity Current mental status Respiratory status Blood glucose Temperature Trauma Medication history Known seizure disorder Possible toxicologic cause Potential causes include: Fever Epilepsy Hypoglycemia Hypoxia Electrolyte abnormalities Infection Trauma Toxicologic exposure Active prolonged seizure activity requires treatment according to the current pediatric seizure protocol. 25. Pediatric Altered Mental Status Potential causes include: Hypoglycemia Hypoxia Seizure Infection Trauma Toxicologic exposure Metabolic abnormalities Intracranial pathology Shock Medication effects A systematic evaluation should include: Airway Breathing Circulation Oxygenation Blood glucose Temperature Neurologic assessment Trauma assessment Medication/toxin history 26. Pediatric Fever and Infection Assess: Temperature Mental status Perfusion Respiratory status Hydration Skin findings Heart rate Blood pressure Capillary refill when appropriate Consider serious infection when fever is associated with: Altered mental status Poor perfusion Respiratory distress Hypotension Petechiae/purpura Severe lethargy Seizure Significant dehydration Follow the local pediatric sepsis/infection protocol. 27. Pediatric Dehydration Potential findings include: Dry mucous membranes Decreased urine output Poor oral intake Tachycardia Weak pulses Delayed capillary refill Altered mental status Abnormal skin findings Potential causes include: Vomiting Diarrhea Fever Poor intake Burns Heat illness Assess severity before determining treatment. 28. Pediatric Trauma The pediatric trauma assessment should address: Airway Breathing Circulation Neurologic status Exposure Mechanism Injury pattern Bleeding Head injury Spinal injury Chest injury Abdominal injury Extremity injury Burns Pediatric patients have anatomical and physiologic differences that may alter injury patterns and treatment. Use the applicable pediatric trauma protocol. 29. Pediatric Head Injury Assess: Mechanism Level of consciousness Pupils Vomiting Seizure Behavior changes Headache Neurologic deficits Signs of skull injury Anticoagulant exposure when relevant Monitor for deterioration during transport. 30. Pediatric Burns Assess: Burn mechanism Burn depth Burn extent Location Airway involvement Inhalation injury Associated trauma Temperature Perfusion Special attention should be given to burns involving: Face Neck Chest Hands Feet Genitals Major joints Follow the applicable pediatric burn protocol. 31. Drowning After a drowning event, prioritize: Ventilation Oxygenation Airway

Anticoagulant exposure when relevant Monitor for deterioration during transport. 30. Pediatric Burns Assess: Burn mechanism Burn depth Burn extent Location Airway involvement Inhalation injury Associated trauma Temperature Perfusion Special attention should be given to burns involving: Face Neck Chest Hands Feet Genitals Major joints Follow the applicable pediatric burn protocol. 31. Drowning After a drowning event, prioritize: Ventilation Oxygenation Airway management CPR when indicated Hypothermia assessment Trauma assessment Reassessment for respiratory deterioration The 2025 AHA special-circumstances guidelines include specific recommendations for drowning-related resuscitation. 32. Toxicologic Emergencies Pediatric toxicologic emergencies may involve: Medications Household chemicals Carbon monoxide Recreational substances Pesticides Opioids Alcohol Hydrocarbons Unknown substances Obtain, when possible: Substance Amount Time of exposure Route Patient weight Symptoms Container/packaging information The 2025 AHA special-circumstances guidance addresses multiple poisoning scenarios, including opioids, beta-blockers, calcium-channel blockers, cyanide, digoxin, organophosphates, sodium-channel blockers, sympathomimetics, and others. 33. Pediatric Medication Safety Pediatric medications require particular attention to: Patient weight Medication concentration Weight-based dosing Maximum dose Route Administration rate Medication concentration Calculation accuracy Equipment size The AI should never estimate a pediatric medication dose when the required weight, indication, or protocol information is unavailable. The 2025 PALS guidelines specifically include weight-based medication administration and dosing during pediatric resuscitation. 34. Weight When medication dosing or fluid therapy is weight-dependent, obtain an actual measured weight when feasible. If an actual weight is unavailable: Follow the local EMS-approved weight-estimation method. Clearly identify that the weight is estimated. Do not present an estimated weight as an actual weight. The AI should distinguish: Actual weight from Estimated weight and should preserve the source of the weight in its response. 35. Reassess: Airway Respiratory effort Oxygenation Ventilation Heart rate Rhythm Blood pressure Perfusion Mental status Temperature Pain Response to treatment A child who initially appears stable may deteriorate rapidly. 40. Determine whether they apply to different indications. Determine whether one is an agency protocol and the other is general guidance. Prefer the current authoritative local protocol. Prehospital Medication Management 1. Purpose This document provides a structured framework for medication use in the prehospital environment. It is designed to support a documentation-grounded paramedic AI by organizing medication information into consistent categories: Indications Contraindications Precautions Dose Route Concentration Administration rate Repeat dosing Maximum dose Expected effects Adverse effects Drug interactions Special populations Monitoring Reassessment Documentation Current local EMS protocols, medical-director orders, approved formulary, scope of practice, pharmacy guidance, manufacturer labeling, and applicable law take precedence over this general reference. 2. Medication Source Hierarchy When answering medication questions, the AI should prioritize sources in the following order: Priority 1 — Current local EMS protocol The local EMS agency or medical director should be the controlling source for: Whether a paramedic may administer a medication Indications Contraindications Dose Concentration Route Repeat dosing Maximum dose Medical-control requirements Pediatric dosing Medication substitutions Required monitoring Scope of practice Priority 2 — Current medication/formulary documentation Use the agency's current medication formulary, medication cards, pharmacy documents, and approved standing orders. Priority 3 — Manufacturer labeling Use current manufacturer information for: Preparation Concentration Administration Compatibility Storage Warnings Contraindications Adverse reactions Priority 4 — Current clinical guidelines Use current authoritative clinical guidelines for evidence-based treatment recommendations. The 2025 AHA guidelines contain current recommendations for pharmacologic treatment during adult cardiac arrest and cardiovascular emergencies. Priority 5 — General medical knowledge General model knowledge should never override a current authoritative local medication protocol. 3. Required Medication Record Every medication placed in the medication folder should ideally contain the following fields: Medication Name: Generic Name: Brand Name: Medication Class: Mechanism: Indications: Contraindications: Precautions: Adult Dose: Pediatric Dose: Geriatric Considerations: Pregnancy Considerations: Route: Concentration: Administration Rate: Repeat Dose: Maximum Dose: Onset: Duration: Expected Effects: Common Adverse Effects: Serious Adverse Effects: Drug Interactions: Relevant Reversal Agent: Required Monitoring: Special Considerations: Protocol Source: Protocol Version: Effective Date: Expiration/Review Date: 4. Medication Verification Before administering a medication, verify: Correct patient Correct medication Correct indication Correct dose Correct concentration Correct route Correct timing Correct administration rate Allergies Relevant contraindications Relevant medication interactions Expiration date Medication integrity Appropriate monitoring Use an independent medication check when required

Interactions: Relevant Reversal Agent: Required Monitoring: Special Considerations: Protocol Source: Protocol Version: Effective Date: Expiration/Review Date: 4. Medication Verification Before administering a medication, verify: Correct patient Correct medication Correct indication Correct dose Correct concentration Correct route Correct timing Correct administration rate Allergies Relevant contraindications Relevant medication interactions Expiration date Medication integrity Appropriate monitoring Use an independent medication check when required by agency policy. 5. Medication Administration Medication administration should occur according to the applicable protocol and medication-specific requirements. Consider: Patient condition Indication Contraindications Route Vascular access Dose Concentration Administration rate Compatibility Monitoring requirements Expected response Potential adverse effects Do not delay life-saving interventions while performing unnecessary medication-related tasks. 6. Medication Routes Common prehospital routes include: IV Used when rapid systemic medication delivery is required and appropriate vascular access is available. IO May be used when IV access cannot be rapidly obtained or is not feasible, according to the applicable protocol. The 2025 AHA adult cardiac-arrest guidelines recommend attempting IV access first for drug administration and consider IO access reasonable when IV access is unsuccessful or not feasible. IM Useful for medications where rapid absorption through muscle is appropriate. Examples may include certain medications used for: Anaphylaxis Hypoglycemia Behavioral emergencies Opioid toxicity Other protocol-specific conditions IN Intranasal administration may be useful when vascular access is unavailable or undesirable. PO / Oral Appropriate only when the patient's condition, airway protection, level of consciousness, and medication indication permit oral administration. SL / Sublingual Used for medications specifically intended for sublingual administration. Nebulized / Inhaled Used for selected respiratory medications. ET Routine medication administration through an endotracheal tube should not be assumed to be an acceptable route. Current resuscitation guidance has removed endotracheal drug administration because drug absorption is unreliable. 7. Cardiac Medications The folder should contain dedicated documents for medications such as: Adenosine Amiodarone Atropine Diltiazem Metoprolol Nitroglycerin Aspirin Other medications authorized by the local cardiac protocol Each medication should specify which rhythms or clinical conditions it is intended to treat. For example, current AHA guidance supports atropine for adults with acute symptomatic bradycardia associated with hemodynamic compromise and describes additional therapies when bradycardia remains unstable despite atropine. 9. Respiratory Medications Include medication references for: Albuterol Ipratropium Epinephrine Steroids Magnesium when specifically indicated Other bronchodilators authorized by local protocol Each respiratory medication should distinguish between conditions such as: Asthma COPD Anaphylaxis Upper-airway disease Other causes of bronchospasm 10. Anaphylaxis Medications The anaphylaxis medication reference should address: Epinephrine Adjunctive antihistamines Corticosteroids Bronchodilators Other protocol-approved medications The AI should identify epinephrine as the primary treatment for anaphylaxis when indicated, rather than presenting adjunctive medications as equivalent alternatives. Special-circumstance resuscitation guidance from the AHA includes specific recommendations for anaphylaxis. 11. Analgesia The analgesia section should include medication-specific information for authorized analgesics. For each medication, include: Indications Pain severity considerations Dose Route Contraindications Respiratory-depression risk Hemodynamic effects Sedation Drug interactions Reassessment requirements The AI should distinguish analgesia from sedation. 12. Sedation Sedation medications should have dedicated references addressing: Indications Contraindications Dose Route Onset Duration Respiratory effects Hemodynamic effects Monitoring Rescue requirements Any medication capable of producing significant respiratory depression should be associated with an airway-management and monitoring reference. 13. Medication-Assisted Airway Management If the local EMS system permits drug-assisted airway management, include separate medication documents for: Induction agents Paralytics Post-intubation analgesia Post-intubation sedation These documents should be linked to the airway folder. medication capable of producing significant respiratory depression should be associated with an airway-management and monitoring reference. 13. Medication-Assisted Airway Management If the local EMS system permits drug-assisted airway management, include separate medication documents for: Induction agents Paralytics Post-intubation analgesia Post-intubation sedation These documents should be linked to the airway folder. The medication AI should never provide an airway medication in isolation when the question involves RSI/DAAM. It should also retrieve the relevant: Airway protocol Patient-selection criteria Preoxygenation requirements Monitoring requirements Rescue-airway requirements Post-intubation management 14. Hypoglycemia Medications Include references for: Oral glucose Dextrose Glucagon Other protocol-approved therapies The AI should determine whether the patient can safely receive an oral medication before recommending oral glucose. Assessment should include: Blood glucose Mental status Ability to protect the airway Ability to swallow Cause of hypoglycemia Response to treatment 15. Opioid Toxicity Include a dedicated naloxone reference. It should address: Indications Routes Initial dosing according to local protocol Repeat dosing Monitoring Recurrent respiratory depression Precipitated withdrawal Need for ventilation Co-ingestants Naloxone should not be treated as a substitute for airway management and ventilation when respiratory failure is present. The 2025 AHA BLS guidelines incorporate opioid antagonists into the cardiac- and respiratory-arrest algorithms, with additional guidance in the special-circumstances section. 16. Seizure Medications The seizure medication section should include authorized medications for: Active seizure Status epilepticus Recurrent seizure activity Each medication should include: Weight-based dosing where applicable Route Maximum dose Respiratory effects Sedation Monitoring Re-dosing requirements Special populations The AI should distinguish an actively seizing patient from a patient with a previous seizure who is now postictal. 17. Behavioral Emergency Medications For medications used in severe agitation or behavioral emergencies, include: Indications Assessment requirements Contraindications Medication selection Dose Route Sedation depth Respiratory monitoring Cardiac monitoring when required Physical-restraint considerations Post-medication reassessment Medication should never replace assessment for potentially reversible medical causes of altered behavior. 18. Shock and Hemodynamic Medications The folder may include medications such as: Epinephrine Norepinephrine Dopamine Other vasopressors authorized by local protocol Each medication should identify: Type of shock Indication Dose Route Infusion preparation Titration Blood-pressure goals when specified by protocol Extravasation

when required Physical-restraint considerations Post-medication reassessment Medication should never replace assessment for potentially reversible medical causes of altered behavior. 18. Shock and Hemodynamic Medications The folder may include medications such as: Epinephrine Norepinephrine Dopamine Other vasopressors authorized by local protocol Each medication should identify: Type of shock Indication Dose Route Infusion preparation Titration Blood-pressure goals when specified by protocol Extravasation considerations Monitoring Exact infusion concentrations and dosing must come from the current local protocol. 19. Toxicology Medications Create dedicated references for medications used for: Opioid toxicity Organophosphate poisoning Beta-blocker toxicity Calcium-channel-blocker toxicity Tricyclic/sodium-channel-blocker toxicity Cyanide toxicity Digoxin toxicity Local-anesthetic systemic toxicity Methemoglobinemia Sympathomimetic toxicity The 2025 AHA special-circumstances guidelines specifically address multiple toxicologic emergencies and their resuscitation management. 20. Electrolyte-Related Medications Include dedicated references for situations involving: Hyperkalemia Hypokalemia Hypomagnesemia Hypocalcemia Other clinically significant electrolyte abnormalities The AI should not recommend calcium, bicarbonate, magnesium, or other electrolyte therapies merely because a cardiac arrest is occurring. The indication must be established. The 2025 AHA guidelines specifically distinguish routine cardiac-arrest medication use from treatment of selected conditions such as hyperkalemia. 21. Medication Contraindications Contraindications should be separated into: Absolute contraindications Conditions in which the medication should not be administered. Relative contraindications Conditions requiring risk-benefit assessment or medical direction. Precautions Conditions requiring additional monitoring or altered administration. The AI should avoid treating a precaution as an absolute contraindication unless the controlling protocol explicitly does so. 22. Medication Interactions Each medication reference should identify clinically significant interactions. Consider: Additive hypotension Additive respiratory depression QT prolongation Bradycardia Tachycardia CNS depression Serotonergic interactions Anticoagulant interactions Renal clearance Hepatic metabolism Drug toxicity When a potential interaction exists, the AI should explain the concern rather than simply stating that an interaction exists. 23. Pediatric Medications Pediatric medication references should be kept separate from adult references whenever possible. Each pediatric medication document should include: Weight-based dosing Maximum dose Concentration Route Equipment considerations Age-specific considerations Weight-estimation method if applicable Reassessment requirements Pediatric medication information should be sourced from the current pediatric EMS protocol. The AHA pediatric guidelines include dedicated recommendations for drug administration and weight-based dosing during pediatric resuscitation. 24.

Medication Errors Potential medication errors include: Wrong patient Wrong medication Wrong concentration Wrong dose Wrong route Wrong administration rate Duplicate administration Failure to recognize contraindication Expired medication Incorrect dilution Incorrect infusion preparation If a medication error occurs, follow the applicable agency medication-error and medical-control procedures. 25. Adverse Medication Reactions After medication administration, monitor for: Hypotension Hypertension Bradycardia Tachycardia Dysrhythmia Respiratory depression Bronchospasm Altered mental status Allergic reaction Anaphylaxis Seizure Extrapyramidal effects Nausea/vomiting Local tissue injury Severe adverse reactions require immediate reassessment and treatment according to the applicable protocol. 26. Medication Reassessment After administration, reassess: Vital signs Mental status Respiratory status Oxygenation Cardiac rhythm Symptoms Pain Blood glucose when applicable Medication-specific endpoints Adverse effects Document the patient's response. A medication should not be considered successful merely because it was administered. 27. Medication Documentation Document: Medication name Dose Concentration Route Administration time Administration rate when relevant Indication Patient response Repeat doses Total dose Adverse effects Medical-control contact when applicable For infusions, document: Medication Concentration Starting rate Titration Rate changes Clinical response 28. AI Medication Answering Rules When a user asks: "What dose of ___ do I give?" The AI should first determine: Patient age Adult vs pediatric Weight when relevant Indication Route Current local protocol Medication concentration Contraindications Relevant clinical circumstances The AI should not provide a dose based solely on the medication name. 29. Check whether the indication differs. Check whether the route differs. Check whether the concentration differs. Flag the discrepancy. The AI should not silently choose one dose when authoritative documents conflict. Recommended response: "The supplied documents contain conflicting dosing information. The current

Missing Information If required medication information is absent, the AI should explicitly state what is missing. Example: "The provided medication documents identify epinephrine as an approved medication but do not provide the applicable dose for this indication." The AI should not fill missing information from memory when the system is intended to be documentation-grounded. 31. Although older SGAs like the Combitube were developed as primary airway devices, historically paramedics were typically instructed to prioritize use of ETI and only used SGAs as rescue devices. Several studies support use of SGAs as rescue air- ways in the setting of failed ETI ( 4, 5). Over the past decade three factors have helped to shift use of SGAs from a role as rescue devices for failed ETI to a role as the primary airway interven- tion in the EMS setting: 1) newer, functionally superior devices (King LTS-D, i-gel, and various LMAs), 2) better recognition of the pitfalls of ETI in the EMS setting, and 3) several randomized con- trolled trials that demonstrated better outcomes and faster processes of care with SGA over ETI in out- of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA). There is mixed evidence that using SGAs may be more easily and rapidly placed than ETTs ( 6, 7). In contrast to Frascone et al. who found no difference in success rate or time to insertion when comparing the King LTS-D to ETI, Russi et al. identified that placement of a Combitube is faster than ETI ( 8, 9). The ease and speed of SGA insertion is likely dependent on features of the device and the compe- tency of the EMS clinician as shown by Russi et al. who showed that insertion of a Combitube is slower than that of a single lumen SGA and by March et al. who showed that i-gel insertion was faster than the King LT ( 8, 10). Studies by Jarvis et al., Bernhard et al., and Middleton et al. have also shown that the success of SGA placement, including both first-pass and overall success rates, varies between different SGA devices ( 11–13). Though these studies suggest that various device-specific factors may affect training needs and successful use, no studies have demonstrated the superiority of any particular SGA device. AVAILABILITY OF SGA D EVICES EMS agencies that perform endotracheal intubation must also equip their clinicians with SGA devices and ensure adequate training and competence. EMS ETI success rates range from 53% to 90%, indi- cating that a substantial portion of cases will require management with rescue airway interventions (22–25). Though all EMS clinicians should be facile with manual ventilation using a bag-valve-mask device, there are circumstances where BVM use may prove difficult ( 26). Historically some EMS agencies have also used surgical airway techniques as a backup strategy for failed ETI; however, these are difficult to perform, even for the most experi- enced clinicians. DRUG ASSISTED SGA I NSERTION In select situations, drug assisted airway management may be used by properly credentialed EMS clinicians to facilitate SGA insertion. Drug-assisted airway management, which includes more commonly known rapid sequence intubation (RSI), also includes Rapid Sequence Airway (RSA), the concept of using sedative and paralytic medica- tions to facilitate SGA insertion by ALS clinicians. Series reported by Frascone and Braude affirm the safety and effectiveness of RSA ( 30–33). The most recent and largest case series published by Braude et al. reported a success rate of 94% and aspiration rates equivalent to other methods of emergency air- way management ( 33). The potential ease and speed of SGA insertion vs ETI may make it easier to achieve first-pass success with RSA than RSI and may help reduce hypoxemia and airway trauma associated with prolonged and repeated intubation attempts (34). The potential disadvantages of RSA include more difficult ventilation via an SGA if high airway pres- sures are required, inability to access the airway reli- ably for suction, and perceptions that SGAs are less effective in protecting against aspiration than endo- tracheal tubes. The risk of aspiration with SGA is lower than previously thought. Several studies suggest that if aspiration occurs it likely happens before inva- sive airway placement rather than during or following insertion (35–41). Second-generation SGAs with gastric aspiration lumens allow for evacuation of gastric con- tents, further reducing the risk for aspiration. CONFIRMATION OF SGA P LACEMENT Confirmation of initial and continuous SGA placement using waveform capnography is strongly encouraged as a best practice. Extensive data inform the requirement for inde- pendent confirmation of ETT placement using wave- form capnography and other subjective and objective measures of successful placement ( 43–45). Despite this emphasis on ETT confirmation, and possibly because of the simplicity of most SGA insertion techniques, many programs have placed relatively little attention on confirmation of SGA placement. However, emerging case reports and ser- ies highlight the pitfalls of SGA placement, includ- ing airway malposition or misplacement ( 1, 46, 47). Though initial confirmation of device location is important SGA dislodgement after initial successful placement is possible. These considerations motivate the recommendation for SGA placement confirm- ation both immediately after insertion and on a con- tinuing basis. Common methods for confirming SGA placement include

While recommended by some experts, colori- metric end-tidal carbon dioxide detection is unre- liable for confirming SGA placement. First, it is possible to qualitatively detect enough residual carbon dioxide through an SGA to result in a “positive ” colorimetric result even when the pos- ition of the device is suboptimal. Second, colori- metric EtCO 2 devices can give false-positive results in some settings and are not reliable if they become contaminated with liquids ( 48–50). Therefore, qualitative colorimetric EtCO 2 detection should not be used in isolation to assess the proper position and function of an SGA on either an initial or ongoing basis. The use of devices that provide continuous quantitative capnometry may help avoid these pitfalls of colorimetric devices, though there are no focused studies on use of such technology by BLS clinicians. Although pulse oximetry is typically accessible to both BLS and ALS clinicians, determination of SGA placement should be based on assessment of adequate ventilation, not oxygen saturation. Poor oxygenation in the setting of adequate ventilation through an SGA usually indicates a failed oxygen supply or respiratory pathology resulting in a shunt, V/Q mismatch, or disordered diffusion, not dys- function of the SGA itself. Additionally, pulse oxim- etry is limited by a significant lag-time between onset of inadequate ventilation and drops in pulse oximetry values ( 51–54). Also, failure to recognize that an SGA may be properly placed and providing appropriate ventilation despite low pulse oximetry values may lead to premature removal of a func- tioning invasive airway ( 55). CONVERSION OF AN SGA TO AN ETT When it is functioning properly, EMS clinicians should refrain from converting an SGA to an endotracheal tube. The decision to convert an SGA to an ET tube must consider the patient ’s condition, the effectiveness of SGA ventilations, and the clinical context and course of initial SGA insertion. If functioning properly, prehospital SGAs should not be exchanged for an ET tube in the prehospital setting. If an SGA is not properly ventilating and the function of the SGA cannot be improved via immediate troubleshooting the EMS clinician should remove the SGA and begin manual ventilation using a bag-valve-mask. In very rare circumstances exchange of a SGA for an ETT may be considered. Clinical scenarios that might favor exchange include the need for high ventilation pressures, the need for tracheal suctioning, presence of copious oropharyngeal secretions, bleeding, or emesis, and anticipated swelling below the level of the SGA that might eventually render it ineffective for ventilation. While SGAs have been associated with significant airway swelling after prolonged placement, devel- opment of this complication typically requires sev- eral hours and prolonged transport is rarely an indication for SGA exchange. Complications related to duration of SGA placement have been reported by Gaither et al. for the King LT at 3 hours and by Gerstein et al. for the LMA-Fastrach at 5 hours. Braude et al. reported there were no complications associated with an LMA-Supreme SGA being left in place for 9 hours ( 57–59). Any clinician considering SGA-ETT exchange should first determine why the SGA was originally placed. This is especially true if an SGA was placed as a rescue device after failed ETI attempts because if the patient

SGA T RAINING AND CLINICAL USE SGA training, competency, and clinical use must be continuously evaluated by EMS agencies using focused quality management programs. Supraglottic airway use is a low-frequency, high risk intervention that should be subject to the same rigorous quality management practices that are used to oversee endotracheal intubation in the EMS setting, including use of high-quality training ses- sions and focused application of quality manage- ment programs to help reduce risk and improve patient outcomes. SGA quality management pro- grams must ensure that clinicians receive appropri- ate training, that they are periodically assessed for their cognitive, psychomotor, and affective competencies related to SGA use, and that clinical use is providing appropriate patient benefit while minimizing patient harms. The principles of preho- spital airway management training and education and quality management of prehospital airway programs, including pediatric-focused topics, are discussed in companion documents to this manu- script, but certain SGA-specific concepts deserve further discussion. Training and Competency. In order to safely and cor- rectly utilize an SGA an EMS clinician must first demonstrate competency in several domains. These include the cognitive domain pertaining to recogni- tion of SGA indications, contraindications, and com- plications; and the psychomotor domain pertaining to delivery of oxygen via nasal cannulas and face- masks, manual bag-valve-mask ventilation, oro/ nasopharyngeal airway placement, and upper air- way suctioning. A number of studies have investigated the ability of EMS clinicians to perform SGA insertion, though many of these studies are limited to manikin-based training encounters ( 78–86). Notably, not all training manikins are alike, as some models are easier or harder for SGA insertion depending on the make/ model of SGA being used ( 87). Further, successful SGA placement in a manikin may not translate to

Further, successful SGA placement in a manikin may not translate to successful use on actual patients. A few studies have evaluated insertion of various SGA devices by different EMS clinicians on anesthetized patients in the operating room, however access to such clinical settings for purposes of EMS clinician training has become increasingly limited ( 12, 88, 89). Training in the use of SGAs requires more than developing a psychomotor skill. EMS clinicians must also receive education in cognitive and critical thinking domains including knowledge of indica- tions and contraindications for SGA use as defined in local protocol, recognition of and mitigation strat- egies for SGA malfunctions, and awareness of potential complications related to SGA use. Competency in less-invasive airway management strategies must also be demonstrated as entry-level proficiencies prior to embarking on SGA education and clinical use. Unfortunately published studies have typically focused only on the psychomotor component of SGA insertion in artificial environ- ments and also have not assessed EMS clinician cog- nitive aptitudes pertaining to SGA use. This makes it difficult to extrapolate whether these studies sup- port whether clinicians can perform SGA insertion in actual clinical practice. Further, attrition of cogni- tive knowledge and decay of psychomotor skill are significant issues that affect the successful use of 36 PREHOSPITAL EMERGENCY CARE JANUARY 2022 V OLUME 26 / N UMBER S1 SGAs by EMS clinicians. However, studies by Fischer et al., Ruetzler et al., and Maddocks have shown that rates of skill decay may be affected by which type of SGA is being used and may be slower than decay of ETI skills ( 90–92). In addition to establishing robust training and monitoring per- formance of EMS clinicians in successfully inserting SGAs, quality management programs should also maintain surveillance for potential complications of SGA use. A case series by Bernhard et al. describes several complications associated with King-style SGAs including airway obstruction due to inadvert- ent tracheal intubation, massive tongue and pharyn- geal edema, air-leak associated hypoventilation, and device obstruction by foreign material ( 93). Other case reports of SGA-related injuries occurring in the prehospital and surgical settings include hypophar- yngeal perforation, pneumomediastinum, subcuta- neous emphysema, pneumoperitoneum, pneumothorax, upper airway bleeding, esophageal laceration or perforation, and pressure-related tissue injuries of the tongue, pharynx, and hypopharyng- eal structures. ( 47, 94–98). Notably the Combitube has been shown to have up to a 40% complication rate ( 95–98). One other important concern related to SGAs is the potential to impair cerebral blood flow. Two swine studies by Segal et al. and Kim et al. that measured carotid artery blood flow during induced cardiac arrest found that the King LTS-D, LMA, Combitube, and i-gel SGAs each significantly reduced carotid blood flow relative to the ETT ( 99, 100). (LMA) found no evidence that either the carotid artery or the internal jugular vein was compressed signifi- cantly ( 103–105). In contrast, Colbert et al. and Zhang et al. showed several different SGAs caused anatomic displacement of the cervical vessels and reduced the velocity of blood flow through them (106, 107). The variable findings of these studies suggest that the effect of SGAs on blood flow through the cervical vessels may be influenced by the design of the SGA (e.g., cuffed vs uncuffed) as well as individual patient-specific factors. Unfortunately, this body of evidence only informs our understanding of the effect of SGAs on the cer- vical vessels and blood flow in hemodynamically stable patients, not on patients with low flow states such as shock or cardiac arrest. There is a significant need for prospective evaluation of cerebral perfu- sion in both hemodynamically stable and unstable patients whose airways are managed with SGAs. Patient Outcomes. Medical directors should under- stand how SGA use may impact clinical outcomes of different patient populations and use this under- standing when developing SGA-related protocols. Cardiac Arrest. Studies by Abo, Wang, and others have shown significantly shorter interruptions in chest compressions during OHCA resuscitation when airways were managed with SGAs compared to ETTs ( 82, 108). Further, the Pragmatic Airway Resuscitation Trial (PART) by Wang et al. demon- strated that 72-hour survival was greater in patients receiving SGAs compared to ETTs ( 109). Secondary outcomes from PART also found increased rates of return of spontaneous circulation, hospital survival, and favorable neurologic exam with SGA manage- ment. However, a subsequent systematic review performed by Carney et al. showed no difference in outcomes when comparing bag-valve-mask manual ventilation, SGAs, and ETT use in OHCA patients (34). Yet another study by Benger et al. also failed to show a survival benefit in OHCA when compar- ing use of the i-gel SGA to ETI ( 110). Finally, the AIRWAYS-2 trial by Benger et al. did not identify a more favorable 30-day functional outcome for

text: outcomes when comparing bag-valve-mask manual ventilation, SGAs, and ETT use in OHCA patients (34). Yet another study by Benger et al. also failed to show a survival benefit in OHCA when compar- ing use of the i-gel SGA to ETI ( 110). Finally, the AIRWAYS-2 trial by Benger et al. did not identify a more favorable 30-day functional outcome for SGAs vs ETI in OHCA ( 110 ). Trauma. Limited studies regarding use of SGAs in the trauma setting have shown potential associa- tions of SGA use with worse patient outcomes, though it is unclear whether this is a reflection of the severity of patient injuries or if there is a more direct connection between outcomes and SGA use (111, 112). FUTURE RESEARCH Future research should attempt to identify which, if any, SGA devices are easiest to use by all levels of EMS clinician, and more importantly, whether any SGA device is superior to others with respect to positively affecting patient outcomes. Research is also needed to help identify techniques to assess SGA function and placement that are accessible to all levels of EMS clinician. Further, studies J. W. Lyng et al. P REHOSPITAL SUPRAGLOTTIC AIRWAYS 37 investigating the best methods for exchanging SGAs for ETTs in the emergency department should also be conducted. Finally, there is a critical need for prospective research regarding the safety of SGAs in the EMS setting, especially their effect on cerebral blood flow in low-flow states such as shock and car- diac arrest. CONCLUSION In summary, SGAs can be used as a reasonable alternative to ETT by ALS clinicians and may expand the ability of BLS clinicians to perform bet- ter ventilation and oxygenation of certain patients. However, data regarding patient-based outcomes of SGAs compared to use of a bag-valve-mask or ETT remains mixed, and optimal SGA utilization strat- egies have yet to be fully defined. ORCID John W. Abstract Although pediatric airway and respiratory emergencies represent high-acuity situations, the ability of EMS clinicians to effectively manage these patients is hampered by infrequent clinical exposure and shortcomings in pediatric-specific education. Cognitive gaps in EMS clinicians’ understanding of the differences between pediatric and adult airway anatomy and respiratory physiology and pathology, variability in the training provided to EMS clinicians, and decay of the psychomotor skills necessary to safely and effectively manage pediatric patients experiencing respiratory emergencies collectively pose significant threats to the quality and safety of care delivered to pediatric patients. NAEMSP recommends: Pediatric airway education should include discussion of the factors that make pediatric airway management challenging. EMS agencies should provide pediatric-specific education that addresses recognition and treatment of pediatric respiratory distress based upon pathophysiology affecting upper airways, lower airways, cardiovascular systems, or extrinsic causes of disordered breathing. Pediatric airway training should also differentiate between hypoxic and hypercapnic respiratory failure. Education should emphasize that the cognitive and psychomotor skills requisite in management of pediatric respiratory emergencies will differ across patient age groups. EMS clinicians should be provided education and training in technology-dependent children and children and youth with special health care needs. EMS clinicians should receive initial and ongoing education and training in pediatric airway and respiratory conditions that emphasizes the principle of using the least invasive most effective strategies to achieve oxygenation and ventilation. Initial and continuing pediatric-focused education should be structured to maintain EMS clinician competency in the assessment and management of pediatric airway and respiratory emergencies and should be provided on a recurring basis to mitigate the decay of EMS clinicians’ knowledge and skills that occurs due to infrequent field-based clinical exposure. Integration of clinician education programs with quality management programs is essential for the development and delivery of initial and continuing education intended to help EMS clinicians attain and maintain proficiency in pediatric airway and respiratory management. Correcting and maintaining oxygenation, ventilation, and perfusion are critically important elements of care for adult and pediatric patients alike. However, helping EMS clinicians understand some key differences in pediatric versus adult patients may help them recognize a child in respiratory distress and intervene in a timely and appropriate manner. EMS education regarding pediatric respiratory emergencies is variable and often limited by competing interests for education resources including time and funding ( Citation 1). Cognitive gaps are amplified by the challenges of limited exposure in clinical practice. It is necessary to recognize and address these challenges via educational initiatives to develop and maintain competency for both the cognitive and psychomotor skills required to manage pediatric respiratory and airway emergencies. To be most effective these educational initiatives must be paired with and supported by robust quality management programs. Pediatric Airway and Respiratory Characteristics and Assessment Pediatric airway education should include discussion of the factors that make pediatric airway management challenging. Pediatric patients are physiologically and anatomically different from their adult counterparts and fostering the fundamental knowledge of these important differences must be a critical goal of educational initiatives for EMS clinicians. Understanding these differences is crucial to the EMS clinician’s ability to form appropriate primary impressions and to develop therapeutic plans. Physiology From a physiologic standpoint EMS education initiatives should help clinicians understand that children, especially premature infants and young term infants, have a poor oxygen reserve as well as a higher metabolic oxygen demand, and that because of this the ability of pediatric patients to maintain adequate oxygenation rapidly declines in response to the physiologic stressors of infection, inflammation, or injury ( Citation 2). EMS clinicians must be able to apply this knowledge in a clinical setting and recognize that pediatric patients have a much earlier

as well as a higher metabolic oxygen demand, and that because of this the ability of pediatric patients to maintain adequate oxygenation rapidly declines in response to the physiologic stressors of infection, inflammation, or injury ( Citation 2). EMS clinicians must be able to apply this knowledge in a clinical setting and recognize that pediatric patients have a much earlier need for oxygenation and assisted ventilation than adult patients. EMS education initiatives should also help clinicians recognize that hypoxia, desaturation, and bradycardia in children are often late signs of progressive shock, and often signal impending cardiac arrest. Anatomy EMS education initiatives should help clinicians recognize the anatomic differences between pediatric and adult patients and how these differences affect the approach to pediatric airway management. Educating EMS clinicians about these differences can help guide their understanding of why different positioning techniques, equipment sizing, medication dosing, and airway insertion techniques need to be adapted based on the age of the patient. Vialet et al. provide an excellent description of the relationship of head posture to pediatric oropharyngeal structures and how these relationships affect pediatric airway management ( Citation 3). These features also make visualization, placement, and maintenance of correct positioning of invasive airway devices challenging in children. Education programs should also include instruction about the increasing number of surviving premature and dysmorphic infants who often have complex abnormal anatomy. An advisory document by Goyal et al. and a review article by Di Cicco et al. provide further excellent and thorough discussion of age-based anatomic and physiologic differences between pediatric and adult patients, how those differences evolve through growth and development, how those features affect pediatric airway management, and strategies to mitigate those various challenges ( Citation 4, Citation 5). EMS clinicians should be educated to use a consistent and reproducible approach to patient assessment. One such approach is the “pediatric assessment triangle,” a cognitive model that guides clinicians to assess a patient’s work of breathing, circulation, and appearance (see Figure 1). Framing pediatric assessment using the “pediatric assessment triangle” construct has been shown to improve field management of children ( Citation 6). Within this framework, assessing the patient’s work of breathing includes physical examination for visual cues of accessory muscle use, retractions, excessive secretions, head bobbing, and cyanosis or pallor; auditory cues of stertor, stridor, and abnormal lung sounds; and assessment of the quality and rate of respirations. Display full size In addition to these physical examination components, EMS clinicians should also be educated on the use of technology like pulse oximetry and capnography to augment their physical exam and history as this technology can help differentiate between hypoxic and hypercapnic respiratory failure. Importantly, education must emphasize the use of appropriate pediatric-sized pulse-oximetry and capnography equipment, as use of sensors and equipment designed for the adult population may provide false readings when used to assess pediatric patients ( Citation 7–10). When used together, physical examination and diagnostic technology may help the EMS clinician to better identify the severity and possibly the causes of respiratory disturbances ( Citation 11). To reduce the need for invasive interventions, pediatric airway education should also stress early and rapid recognition of respiratory disturbances. Earlier recognition of respiratory issues in the time-course spanning from normal breathing to respiratory/cardiac arrest can likely translate to use of less invasive, easier, and less risk-prone interventions compared to the interventions needed when recognition of respiratory disturbances is delayed. However limited data suggests EMS clinician performance is poor regarding the accurate recognition of pediatric respiratory distress and selection of appropriate interventions. In a study of 420 paramedics completing a multimedia case-based questionnaire, Schroter et al. found that while paramedics could correctly identify respiratory distress severity in 92% of cases, they performed poorly with correct identification of the disease process (50% of cases) and performance of appropriate interventions (38% of cases) ( Citation 12). Categories of Pediatric Respiratory Disturbances EMS agencies should provide pediatric-specific education that addresses recognition and treatment of pediatric respiratory distress based upon pathophysiology affecting upper airways, lower airways, cardiovascular systems, or extrinsic causes of disordered breathing. Pediatric airway training should also differentiate between hypoxic and hypercapnic respiratory failure. Education should emphasize that the cognitive and psychomotor skills requisite in management of pediatric respiratory emergencies will differ across patient age groups. The educational techniques used to help adult learners become competent in the cognitive and psychomotor domains of airway management are discussed in a companion to this document: Prehospital Airway Management Training and Education ( Citation 13). In addition to using these strategies, dividing pediatric respiratory disturbances into four categories may help some learners to differentiate between the potential causes of pediatric respiratory distress and to implement appropriate treatment protocols. Upper Airway Disturbances Key education includes awareness of nasopharynx-related causes of respiratory distress, including that infants 4 months of age and under are obligate nose breathers, and as such simple upper respiratory infections can result in nasal obstruction and respiratory failure. In patients with bronchiolitis, nasal suctioning is a minimally invasive treatment that can rapidly improve respiratory distress. Other areas for educational emphasis include proper nasopharyngeal airway sizing and placement. In addition to nasopharyngeal issues, younger pediatric patients and patients with various congenital diagnoses may have larger tongues,

such simple upper respiratory infections can result in nasal obstruction and respiratory failure. In patients with bronchiolitis, nasal suctioning is a minimally invasive treatment that can rapidly improve respiratory distress. Other areas for educational emphasis include proper nasopharyngeal airway sizing and placement. In addition to nasopharyngeal issues, younger pediatric patients and patients with various congenital diagnoses may have larger tongues, smaller jaws, larger occiputs, and increased secretions that may also impede airway patency ( Citation 5). Further, children often present with stridor due to anatomic subglottic narrowing and smaller diameter of the trachea. Multiple diagnoses can lead to stridor including infectious processes, congenital malformations, anaphylactic reactions, or foreign body obstruction. Education on airway positioning, jaw thrusting, suctioning, proper selection of oropharyngeal airway size and indications for use, and selection of inhaled medications appropriate for treatment of stridor are recommended. Lower Airway Disturbances Younger pediatric patients, especially infants and toddlers, have key lower anatomical distinctions such as smaller bronchiolar passages, flexible cartilaginous ribs, smaller lung volumes, and lower oxygen reserves. Lower airway-focused education should guide EMS clinicians to perform examination of the entire ribcage of younger patients to assess for intercostal, supraclavicular, and subcostal retractions. Further, EMS clinicians should be educated that smaller lower airway structures trap mucus more easily, which can cause patients with bronchiolitis to have wheezing that sounds like expiratory rales. EMS clinicians should be able to differentiate these sounds from the inspiratory rales associated with pneumonia or pulmonary edema. Mixed Upper/Lower Airway Disturbances: Bronchiolitis and Anaphylaxis Some conditions such as bronchiolitis and anaphylaxis can affect both upper and lower airways simultaneously, and clinicians should be educated to recognize they may need to tailor their interventions to address both anatomic regions. For example, in addition to providing a trial of nebulized albuterol for a wheezing bronchiolitis patient with respiratory distress, it is also key to educate the EMS clinician regarding recognition of obstructed nasal passages and the proper techniques for performing nasal suctioning. Although anaphylaxis most commonly manifests with wheezing and hives in pediatric patients, it can also present with stridor. Studies by Tiyagura et al. and Carrillo

Although anaphylaxis most commonly manifests with wheezing and hives in pediatric patients, it can also present with stridor. Studies by Tiyagura et al. and Carrillo et al. confirm that rates of EMS clinician recognition of pediatric anaphylaxis are poor ( Citation 14, Citation 15). Because treatment of anaphylaxis differs from other causes of pediatric stridor and wheezing, it is critical for EMS education initiatives to help clinicians differentiate anaphylaxis from other conditions. Cardiovascular Pathologies EMS pediatric education should also address pediatric cardiovascular conditions that may present with acute respiratory distress. Information obtained from the patient’s caregivers may help the EMS clinician recognize congenital cardiovascular conditions including persistent pulmonary hypertension (commonly associated with severe prematurity), single ventricle cardiac defects with staged repairs, and cyanotic congenital heart disorders. EMS clinicians should be educated on the importance of working with the guardians who are aware of the patient’s baseline, early notification to the hospital, and when possible, transporting the patient to a hospital within the patient’s medical home. The EMS clinician should also be aware of acute cardiac etiologies that may present as respiratory distress, such as supraventricular tachycardia and myocarditis, and how to assess and intervene in these scenarios. Extrinsic Causes of Disordered Breathing EMS clinician education should emphasize recognition of and intervention for three important presentations of extrinsic causes of disordered breathing: Apnea: All EMS clinicians should be educated to rapidly recognize absence of respiratory effort during physical exam and through identification of absent or low-amplitude waveforms on capnography when this technology is available. Clinicians should also be educated that pulse oximetry may not demonstrate hypoxia for several minutes after the onset of apnea and that apnea should be treated with immediate use of manual BVM ventilation prior to attempts at invasive airway insertion. Respiratory Alkalosis-related tachypnea: EMS clinicians should be aware that patients with metabolic acidosis from various causes often develop a compensatory respiratory alkalosis

also be educated that pulse oximetry may not demonstrate hypoxia for several minutes after the onset of apnea and that apnea should be treated with immediate use of manual BVM ventilation prior to attempts at invasive airway insertion. Respiratory Alkalosis-related tachypnea: EMS clinicians should be aware that patients with metabolic acidosis from various causes often develop a compensatory respiratory alkalosis that can be differentiated from other causes of tachypnea by identifying concomitant low EtCO2 values. To maintain this compensatory state, clinicians should be educated regarding the critical need to match or exceed these patient’s tachypneic respiratory rate when initiating manual or mechanical ventilation. Hypoventilatory respiratory failure: EMS clinicians should understand that hypoventilation-induced hypoxia is often caused by head trauma, overt or subclinical status epilepticus, post-ictal states, toxic ingestions, and other conditions. Education should emphasize that relying on pulse oximetry to identify hypoventilation can lead to delayed recognition whereas use of continuous capnography or quantitative capnometry can lead to almost immediate recognition of hypoventilation. Pediatric airway education should also stress early and rapid recognition of respiratory disturbances. Earlier recognition of respiratory issues in the time-course spanning from normal breathing to respiratory/cardiac arrest can likely translate to use of less invasive, easier, and less risk-prone interventions compared to the interventions needed when recognition of respiratory disturbances is delayed. However limited data suggests EMS clinician performance is poor regarding the accurate recognition and treatment of pediatric respiratory distress. In a study of 420 paramedics completing a multimedia case-based questionnaire, Schroter, et al. found that while paramedics could correctly identify respiratory distress severity in 92% of cases, they performed poorly with correct identification of the disease process (50% of cases) and performance of appropriate interventions (38% of cases) ( Citation 12). Participation in specialized educational programs that focus on these patients and the different technologies used in their care can improve EMS clinician comfort and knowledge in providing them care ( Citation 17). Approach to Pediatric Airway and Respiratory Interventions EMS clinicians should receive initial and ongoing education and training in pediatric airway and respiratory conditions that emphasizes the principle of using the least invasive most effective strategies to achieve oxygenation and ventilation. To help achieve improvements in patient safety and outcomes, EMS education initiatives should emphasize the use of the least invasive yet most effective interventions to correct disturbances in airway patency, ventilation, or oxygenation. Many low frequency-high risk procedures such as endotracheal intubation are associated with significant risks to the patient, and in certain cases these risks can be avoided by using less invasive interventions, especially when lower-risk interventions can achieve similar outcomes. For example, recent studies of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest have shown equivalent outcomes for those patients managed with a BVM, a fundamental but challenging low-risk skill to perform, versus those managed with endotracheal intubation, a complex high-risk skill that is even more challenging to master than BVM ventilation ( Citation 18).
